terms.meaning: A huge land area that is part of a continent. India occupies the south of Asia.
Land with water on three sides and land on one side.
The time before writing was discovered, so it has no written records.
A scholar who studies the distant past from the things people left behind.
A person with no settled home, living by hunting and gathering food.
A place where people made stone tools, shown by heaps of broken stone chips.

items.name: Other names of Greater India
items.formula: Bharathavarsha, Bharatha Khanda, Sindhudweepa and Akhandabharatha.
items.example: Today India has 28 states and 8 union territories.

items.name: Countries sharing India's boundary
items.formula: Pakistan, Afghanistan, China, Nepal, Bhutan, Bangladesh and Myanmar.
items.example: Sri Lanka is across the sea, so it is not on this list.

items.name: India's four physical regions
items.formula: The Himalayas, the Indo-Gangetic Plain, the Deccan Plateau and the coast.
items.example: Attacks came mainly from the north-west, through the Bolan and Khyber passes.

items.name: What the Narmada divides
items.formula: The Malwa Plateau (Central Highlands) from the Deccan Plateau in the south.
items.example: This north and south division led to cultural diversity.

items.name: India's coastline
items.formula: 6,100 km on the mainland, and 7,516.60 km with the islands.

items.name: Names of the two coasts
items.formula: East: Coromandel and Utkal. West: Konkan and Malabar.
items.example: Ports on them drew the Romans and helped the Pandyas, Cheras and Cholas rise.

items.name: Pre-historic period
items.formula: Only archaeological remains, with no written records.

items.name: Proto-historic period
items.formula: Remains and writing both exist, but the writing can't be read.

items.name: Historic period
items.formula: Remains and readable written documents both exist.

items.name: Where prehistoric people lived
items.formula: Near rivers and lakes, in areas with plenty of stone for tools.

items.name: Proof that Stone Age people used fire
items.formula: Ash found in the caves of Kurnool.
items.example: Fire probably gave cooking, light and safety from animals.

items.name: Cave drawings
items.formula: Wild animals and hunting, drawn on cave walls and rocks.
items.example: Seen in Madhya Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh and Karnataka.

items.name: How animal husbandry began
items.formula: About 12,000 years ago the earth warmed and grasslands spread, so animals multiplied.
items.example: People watched the animals, captured them and tamed them.

items.name: Old Stone Age
items.formula: The oldest period, from 2 million years ago to 12,000 years ago.
items.example: It has three stages: Early, Middle and Late.

items.name: Middle Stone Age
items.formula: From 12,000 to about 10,000 years ago, with very small "delicate" stone weapons.
items.example: Tiny stones were set in bone or wood handles, as axes and saws.

items.name: New Stone Age
items.formula: After 10,000 years ago, with bright, sharp-bladed tools.
items.example: Grinding stones, pots for grain and cooking, and woven cloth.

mistakes.text: The Indus Valley is proto-historic, not prehistoric: it has writing, but nobody can read it yet.
People also used wood and bone, but mostly only the stone tools have survived.
The order is Old, then Middle, then New. Pots and weaving belong to the New Stone Age.
